name: Full codebase audit for bugs and defects
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The person requested a full codebase audit of a hosting platform repository (Shanutechx-hostingplatfrom-main), asking Claude to read every source file and produce a written bug report in a specific Markdown format saved as `BUG_AUDIT.md` at the repo root. The audit was explicitly read-only — no source files were to be modified. The person's instructions specified finding bugs across categories including logic errors, race conditions, null handling, resource leaks, error handling gaps, security issues, API contract mismatches, and silent failures, with a clear distinction between confirmed and suspected bugs.

The conversation spanned three continuation turns as Claude worked through the codebase systematically, front-loading the highest-risk areas: `apps/api/src/lib/` (all ~44 files), `apps/api/src/middleware/`, `services/node-agent/src/` (all 11 files), and approximately 24 of 49 route files. Claude maintained working scratch notes at `/home/claude/notes/findings.md` across turns to preserve findings when tool call limits were reached. At the end of each turn, Claude summarized confirmed findings in the chat before the final report was written. The person's responses were single-word continuations ("Continue"), indicating they wanted the audit to proceed without interruption until complete.

The final `BUG_AUDIT.md` was written to the repository root and copied to `/mnt/user-data/outputs/BUG_AUDIT.md`. It documented 30 confirmed bugs and 1 suspected issue across 7 Critical, 10 High, 10 Medium, and 3 Low severity levels, covering ~80 first-party source files. The most significant findings included: container resource limits silently never being applied by the node-agent; the Stop/Start lifecycle being completely broken due to force-removal of containers; three independent features reporting fabricated success responses while doing nothing (managed database backup/restore, PR preview deployments, and the `/email/send` webmail endpoint); an open mail relay accessible to any authenticated user via `POST /smtp/send`; an SSRF vector via `POST /smtp/verify`; and an OAuth/magic-link open redirect that leaks authentication tokens to attacker-controlled URLs. A recurring architectural pattern was identified: "fake success" responses (three instances), protections on the main Git deploy path not propagated to zip/Docker alternate paths, and DB status drifting from actual container state across multiple independent bugs. In the final turn, the person asked for a separate report covering the ~25 remaining unreviewed route files, which Claude began auditing — finding additional confirmed bugs in `projectAuth.ts` (open redirect leaking JWTs, unvalidated OAuth email verification), `admin.ts` (policy gap allowing plain admin to create dev-role accounts), and `status.ts` (dev role excluded from uptime endpoint staff access).

chat_messages.text:
You are performing a full codebase audit. Your goal is to read every source file in this repository and produce a written report of all bugs, defects, and hidden/latent issues you find — without fixing anything yet.
Scope
Enumerate every source file in the repository (exclude node_modules, .git, build output, vendored/third-party code, and lockfiles unless specifically asked).
Read each file in full — do not skim or sample. For large files, read them in sequential chunks until the whole file is covered.
Build a mental (or written, if useful) model of the codebase: entry points, module boundaries, data flow, shared state, external calls (network, filesystem, DB), and how modules depend on each other. Many real bugs only show up when you trace a value or side effect across files, not within a single file.
What counts as a "bug"
Look for issues across these categories:
Obvious/functional bugs — logic errors, wrong operators, off-by-one errors, incorrect conditionals, wrong variable used, dead code that should run, unreachable code.
Hidden / latent bugs — issues that don't fail today but will under certain conditions:
Race conditions and unsafe concurrent access (shared mutable state, missing locks/mutexes, async ordering assumptions).
Null/undefined/None handling — missing checks, unsafe optional chaining, implicit type coercion bugs.
Off-by-one and boundary errors in loops, array/string indexing, pagination, date ranges.
Resource leaks — unclosed file handles, DB connections, sockets, listeners, timers/intervals never cleared.
Error handling gaps — swallowed exceptions, empty catch blocks, errors logged but not handled, missing rollback on failure.
Incorrect assumptions about input (unvalidated user input, unchecked array lengths, assuming a list is never empty).
State mutation bugs — mutating shared/passed-in objects, accidental global state, stale closures.
Concurrency/async bugs — unawaited promises, missing await, fire-and-forget calls that should be awaited, unhandled promise rejections.
Security-relevant bugs — injection risks (SQL/command/template), unsafe deserialization, hardcoded secrets/credentials, missing authz/authn checks, insecure defaults.
Type mismatches — especially in dynamically typed languages, or unsafe casts/any usage that hides a real mismatch.
Configuration/environment bugs — values that only break in prod, missing env var validation, inconsistent config across environments.
API/contract mismatches — function signatures that don't match how they're called elsewhere, inconsistent return types, breaking changes not propagated to all callers.
Logic that works for the "happy path" but breaks for edge cases (empty input, max input, duplicate input, concurrent requests, retries).
Copy-paste bugs — code duplicated from elsewhere with a variable/condition not updated correctly.
Silent failures — functions that fail without throwing or logging, masking downstream problems.
Method
Read every file fully before drawing conclusions — don't flag something as a bug based on partial context.
Cross-reference: when you find something suspicious in one file, check where it's called/used elsewhere before deciding it's actually a bug.
Distinguish between confirmed bugs (you can show exactly how they break) and suspected/potential issues (plausible but you can't fully verify without running the code or more context) — do not blur this distinction.
Do not report generic style nitpicks (formatting, naming conventions) unless they directly cause a bug or dangerously obscure one.
For each finding, note why it's a bug — not just what looks off.
Output
Produce a single Markdown report with this structure:

## Audit status — partial results, tool budget reached

I was about two hours into a genuinely full-repo audit (I'd scoped it down to ~458 first-party source files, ~64K LOC, after confirming `packages/{auth-js,postgrest-js,realtime-js,functions-js,storage-js,supabase-js}` are vendored 1:1 forks of the real Supabase SDK repos and excluding them per your instructions). I was moving through `apps/api` and `services/node-agent` in depth when I hit the tool-call limit for this turn, so **`BUG_AUDIT.md` was not generated** and most of the tree (all of `apps/dashboard`, `apps/web`, `apps/mobile-admin`, `packages/{catalog,client,db,deployments,node-agent,types,tracing}`, `services/{whatsapp-bot,discord-bot}`, `infra/`, `templates/`, `tests/`) is unreviewed.

Here's what I confirmed before running out of calls, in case it's useful now — I'd need another turn to finish the sweep and write the actual report file.

**Critical**
1. **Resource limits are never applied to containers.** `services/node-agent/src/index.js`'s `build-and-run` route never forwards `cpuLimit`/`memoryLimit`/`storageLimit` from the request body to `runContainer()`, even though `docker.js` supports them and apps/api sends them on every deploy/redeploy/limit-update. Every container silently runs at the hardcoded default (1 CPU / 512MB), regardless of plan or explicit admin override — `PATCH /deployments/:id/limits` updates the DB and reports success but changes nothing real.
2. **"Stop" permanently breaks "Start."** The deployment-level stop route calls `stopAndRemove()` (force-removes the container), but `containerId` is never cleared, and `/start` tries to start that same now-deleted container ID. Confirmed the dashboard actually offers a Start button whenever status is `stopped`/`failed`. Every stop→start cycle 502s.
3. **Table Editor writes are 100% broken.** `apps/api/routes/projects.ts` proxies insert/update/delete row requests to node-agent routes that were never implemented (`grep` across all `app.post/patch/delete` in node-agent's `index.js` confirms only GET exists). Dashboard wires real Add/Edit/Delete buttons to this dead path; all silently 404.

**High**
4. Node-agent's workspace-cleanup route references `path`/`fs` that are never `require()`d in that file — always throws, always fails, so 24h workspace retention never actually purges anything (disk leak on every node).
5. The shadow-backup "restore after cleanup" path in `repo.js` requires a `remoteBackupUrl` parameter that no caller ever supplies — latent data-loss bug, currently masked by bug #4 but would activate the moment that one's fixed.

**Medium**
6. SQL injection via unvalidated `:table` route param in one node-agent route (missing the `validateIdentifier()` call used elsewhere in the same file) — real, but only reachable by the already-fully-trusted `dev` role.
7. Inconsistent admin visibility rules: `ownedResourceWhere()` (list endpoints) excludes unassigned customers' resources for admin, but `canAccessResource()`/`verifyResourceOwnershipAsync()` (detail/action endpoints) include them — an admin can act on a specific unassigned-customer resource by ID that never shows up in their own list view. Affects ~14 route files.
8. `PATCH /deployments/:id/subdomain` creates a new Cloudflare CNAME but never deletes the old one (orphaned DNS record).
9. `PATCH /deployments/:id/limits` doesn't mark the deployment `status: 'failed'` on a failed restart (unlike the sibling `/redeploy` and `/env` routes), leaving the DB claiming "running" when the container actually failed.

I was mid-review of `cockpit.ts`'s RBAC (looked sound so far — cluster nodes admin/dev-only, VPS scoped to owner via `canAccessResource`) when I stopped.

**Recommendation:** let me continue in a follow-up turn — I'll pick up exactly where I left off (I have working notes on disk at `/home/claude/notes/findings.md`), finish the remaining ~85% of the tree, and produce the actual `BUG_AUDIT.md` deliverable at the repo root as originally requested. Want me to continue now?

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"=== CHANGELOG_fixes_applied.md ===
# ShanuTechX — Fixes Applied (Changelog)

This documents every change made to `shanutechx-source-clean.zip` in response to the code audit, delivered as `shanutechx-source-FIXED.zip`. Findings are referenced by the IDs from the original audit report (C1–C7, H1–H10, M1–M8).

**Before doing anything else: rotate every secret in the original `apps/api/.env`.** Those values were exposed to me as part of this review and must be treated as compromised regardless of anything below. The `.env` files have been stripped from this fixed archive entirely — you'll need to regenerate them from `.env.example` with fresh values.

**Infrastructure/deployment additions (separate from the bug-fix list below):** this pass also added a complete first-time deployment path — MinIO (object storage), a self-hosted Postal mail stack, and fixes to the pre-existing self-hosted Supabase stack (which had no persistent volumes, no working API gateway config, local-disk-only storage, and shipped public demo JWT keys) — wired into both `infra/control-plane/docker-compose.yml` (production, with Traefik/TLS) and the pre-existing `docker/docker-compose.shanutechx.yml` unified dev orchestrator. Also fixed a service-naming collision between Infisical (a bundled but previously-unwired secrets manager) and the other stacks that would have silently broken one of them when run together. Full details in `DEPLOYMENT_GUIDE.md`, not repeated here since it's deployment/infra work rather than an application bug.

---

## 🔴 Critical — all fixed

- **C2** — `GET /api/supabase/config` (leaked the Supabase service-role key to any authenticated user) now requires `requireAdminOrDev`. One-line fix in `routes/supabase.ts`.
- **C4** — `routes/settings.ts` rewritten. The PIN is now a bcrypt hash stored on `User.settingsPinHash` (new migration `20260819000000_settings_pin_hash`), not an in-memory value with a `'123456'`/`'admin'`/any-4-char fallback. Verification fails closed (412) if no PIN has been set — there is no bypass of any kind.
- **C5** — `nodes.ts`'s hardcoded `CLUSTER_SECRET` fallback removed entirely; it now uses the already-`required()` `env.nodeAgentSecret` with a timing-safe HMAC comparison. **This is the fix that matters most to apply before you go live** — rotate `NODE_AGENT_SECRET` to a new value, since the old hardcoded fallback is now public.
- **C6** — Added the missing `GET /agent/deployments/:containerId/metrics` route to `services/node-agent`. While implementing it, found and fixed a second, more severe bug: `docker.js` never actually exported `listContainers`/`startContainer`/`getLogs`/`streamLogs` (only destructured as `undefined` in `index.js`), so the Containers page, log viewer, and live log streaming were all crashing with `TypeError` on every real request. All four are now implemented with `dockerode` (including `modem.demuxStream` for live log streaming).
- **C7** — `apps/api/Dockerfile` now `COPY`s `templates/` into the build and runtime stages — the self-hosted app catalog (WordPress/n8n/MongoDB/Redis/Lavalink/LiveKit) was previously always empty in any Docker deployment. Also unified `catalog.ts` and `catalog-manager.ts` onto the same `__dirname`-relative path resolution (previously one used `process.cwd()`, which is fragile to how the process is launched).

## 🟠 High — all fixed except the H1/H8 persistence backlog (see "Not done" below)

- **H2 / H4 (node-agent)** — timing-safe secret comparison (was `!==`); bind host is now configurable (`AGENT_BIND_HOST`, default unchanged at `0.0.0.0` to avoid breaking existing deployments) with an optional `AGENT_ALLOWED_IPS` allowlist and a loud startup warning if neither is set.
- **H3** — Fixed the WhatsApp/Discord bot Docker networking bug: both now bind to all interfaces inside their own container (was `127.0.0.1`, which silently blocks sibling-container access even via Compose service-name DNS) — this was why WhatsApp/Discord notifications were silently never delivered under `docker-compose.local.yml`. Removed the now-pointless host port publishing for both in `docker-compose.local.yml` (they were never meant to be reachable from the host).
- **H4 (vps-plans.ts)** — delete route now matches `products.ts`'s correct pattern: try hard-delete, catch FK-constraint failures, fall back to `isActive: false` instead of a raw 500. (`catalog.ts`'s delete route was re-examined and found to be a different case — it deletes a template *file*, not a DB row with foreign keys, so the same pattern doesn't actually apply there; left as-is.)
- **H5** — Added `redact` config to both the base `pino` logger and the `pino-http` instance — `Authorization`, `x-agent-secret`, `x-internal-secret`, `x-cron-secret`, `x-webhook-secret`, `x-signature` headers, plus common secret-shaped field names, are no longer written to plaintext logs.
- **H6** — Billing sweep and uptime checks now self-schedule via BullMQ in `worker.ts` (daily at 01:00, and every 5 minutes, respectively), matching the pattern SSL renewal already used. No longer dependent on a `.github/workflows/billing-cron.yml` that never existed. The manual "run checks" endpoints in `routes/billing.ts`/`routes/status.ts` still work too.
- **H7 — rewritten as a real feature, not just a bug fix.** Per your follow-up request, the entire Git-connect flow has been replaced:
  - **GitHub**: a real GitHub App integration. Users install the App and pick repos on GitHub's own UI; we store only the installation ID (`GitHubInstallation` model, new migration). Every API call mints a fresh, short-lived (~1hr) installation access token via a signed App JWT — no PAT, no long-lived token stored anywhere.
  - **GitLab**: a real OAuth application integration (`read_user read_repository` scopes only). Access + refresh tokens are encrypted at rest (`GitLabConnection` model, same migration) and refreshed automatically when expired.
  - Both sit behind a common `GitProviderAdapter` interface (`lib/gitProviders/types.ts`) so a third provider is "implement the interface, register it in `index.ts`" — nothing else changes.
  - A signed, single-use, 5-minute `state` parameter replaces the old raw-user-ID state (fixes the account-linking CSRF weakness).
  - The dashboard's "Connect GitHub/GitLab" now redirects the browser directly to the provider — there is no token-paste modal or input field anywhere in the flow anymore.
  - `routes/deployments.ts` and `routes/filesystem.ts`'s git-push both resolve a scoped token server-side from a connected account ID; `gitToken` is retained only for `gitProvider: 'custom'` (self-hosted git hosts with no App/OAuth integration here).
- **H8** — Solved as a side effect of the H7 rewrite: the old unpersisted, in-memory `gitUserAccounts` map is gone entirely, replaced by the two real, persisted Prisma models above.
- **H9** — Added audit logging to `leaseweb.ts`'s `credentials` and `ssh-ticket` routes (previously the two most sensitive actions in that file left no trail at all). Added a new nullable `AuditLog.actorRole` column (migration `20260819000100_audit_log_actor_role`) so customer self-service actions (like VPS password reset) are distinguishable from genuine staff actions — populated on all three routes now.
- **H10** — Fixed every broken SDK path/shape found in the original audit:
  - `packages/node-agent`: `stopContainer`/`startContainer`/`restartContainer` now call the real `/agent/deployments/:id/{action}` routes.
  - `packages/client`'s `deployments.ts`: `getResourceUsage` now reads from the real detail response instead of a nonexistent `/stats` route; `addDomain`/`removeDomain` now hit the real `/custom-domain` route with the right shape (plus a new `verifyDomain()`); `delete()` now throws a clear, explicit error instead of silently 404ing, since there genuinely is no server-side delete-the-record route (that's a product decision outside the scope of a bug fix — see "Not done" below).
  - `packages/client`'s `git.ts`: rewritten entirely to match the new H7 architecture — `removeAccount` now uses the real `/git/disconnect` endpoint; `resolveAccountForRepo`'s broken `.login` property lookup fixed (`packages/types`' `GitAccount`/`GitRepo` types corrected to match what the API actually returns).

## 🟡 Medium — all fixed

- **M1** — Replaced the reflect-any-Origin-with-credentials CORS middleware with the `cors` package configured against an explicit allowlist (the same one `csrfProtection.ts` already maintained — now shared via `isOriginAllowed()` instead of being duplicated).
- **M2/M3** — `.env.example` updated: documented that `WHATSAPP_BOT_URL`/`DISCORD_BOT_URL` need Compose service names under Docker (not `localhost`), and added the new GitHub App / GitLab OAuth variables.
- **M6** — `billing.ts`'s cron-fallback now allows `dev` role, not just `admin`, matching `requireAdmin`'s behavior everywhere else.
- **M7** — Deleted `lib/verifyPayment.ts.disabled`, `lib/gemini.ts`, `lib/groq.ts` (confirmed dead — nothing imported them) and their now-unused `GEMINI_API_KEY`/`GROQ_API_KEY` env vars.
- **M8** — Fixed the double-mounted `settingsRouter` (was mounted at both `/api/settings` and `/api`, with route paths that happened to paper over it). Now mounted once at `/api/settings` with route paths matching exactly what the dashboard frontend already calls (`verify-password`, `change-pin`, `configs`).

## Templates: hardcoded default passwords — fully fixed, including auto-generation

All six `templates/*.yaml` files (WordPress, n8n, MongoDB, Redis, Lavalink, LiveKit) had weak, now-public default passwords baked in via Compose's `${VAR:-default}` fallback syntax. These have been changed to `${VAR:?VAR must be set}` (Compose's required-variable syntax — fails loudly instead of silently deploying with a known weak password).

`routes/catalog.ts`'s deploy handler now auto-generates a strong random value (`crypto.randomBytes(24).toString('base64url')`) for each of these specific keys whenever the customer doesn't supply one, so a deploy never actually fails because of this — and returns the generated values in the deploy response (`generatedSecrets`) so the customer can save them. This was the piece flagged as incomplete in the previous version of this changelog; it's now done.

## C3 — webmail cross-tenant IDOR — fixed

`routes/webmail.ts` is now backed by a real, per-user-owned `WebmailMessage` Prisma model (migration `20260819000300_webmail_per_user_scoping`) instead of a single global in-memory `Map` shared by every user on the platform. Every route (`list`, `get`, `patch`, `delete`) filters by the authenticated user's own ID — a message belonging to another user simply doesn't match the query and 404s, closing the IDOR.

As part of the same fix, `POST /webmail/send` now sends through the user's actual provisioned `SmtpAccount` credentials (same `encryptSecret`/`decryptSecret` pattern already used correctly in `routes/smtp.ts`/`routes/email.ts`) instead of the old undocumented `SMTP_HOST`/`SMTP_USER`/`SMTP_PASS` env vars with a hardcoded fallback password — this also resolves M4/M5 from the original audit. Delivery failures are now awaited and surfaced to the caller (`502` with the saved draft still returned) instead of silently disappearing into an unawaited background promise.

## H1 — every remaining in-memory store persisted

All four remaining unpersisted, in-memory feature stores identified in the original audit have now been replaced with real Prisma-backed tables, following the same pattern established by the git-provider and webmail rewrites above:

- **Knowledge Base** (`routes/knowledgebase.ts`) — new `KbArticle`/`KbCategory` models (migration `20260819000400_knowledgebase_tables`, seeded with the original demo content so behavior is unchanged immediately after migrating). All CRUD routes rewritten.
- **Global SMTP config + per-account domains/aliases** (`routes/smtp.ts`) — the platform-wide outbound mail config is now a persisted `PlatformSmtpConfig` singleton (password encrypted via `secretsVault`, migration `20260819000500_smtp_persisted_config`); per-account custom domain + alias list now live directly on `SmtpAccount` (new columns in the same migration). The hardcoded fallback password (`'smtp_secret_pass'`) is now only used to seed the config row the very first time it's read, not as a permanent runtime fallback.
- **Custom email domain verification records** (`routes/email.ts`) — new `EmailDomain` model (migration `20260819000600_email_domain_records`).
- **Secrets Vault** (`routes/secrets.ts`) — new `SecretProject`/`SecretItem`/`SecretAuditEntry` models (migration `20260819000700_secrets_vault_tables`). Secret values are now actually encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM via the existing `secretsVault`) — the previous in-memory version stored them as plaintext despite being branded a "vault."
- **Supabase management panel** (`routes/supabase.ts`) — new `SupabaseClientProject`, `SupabaseAuthSmtpConfig`, `SupabaseEmailTemplate`, `SupabaseSmtpDeliveryLog` models (migration `20260819000800_supabase_panel_tables`, seeded with the original demo content/templates). **Scope note:** this only fixes the persistence bug — it does not make the "client projects" into real, separately-provisioned, isolated Supabase stacks (this platform runs one shared Kong/GoTrue/PostgREST stack under the hood). That's a genuine infrastructure project, not a bug fix, and is out of scope here.

All dashboard-facing response shapes were preserved exactly (verified against `lib/api.ts` and `lib/secretsApi.ts`), so no frontend changes were needed for any of these five.

---

## Everything from the original audit is now addressed

Every Critical, High, and Medium finding from the original audit report — including every item raised across all follow-up review passes — has been fixed. What's left is only the "Low / cleanup" tier from the very first version of the audit report:

- The 40 Prisma relations without an explicit `onDelete` (likely intentional, given the soft-delete pattern used elsewhere — worth a confirmation pass, not an urgent fix)
- `CLAUDE.md` claims Next.js 15; the actual pinned version is 14.2.35
- One remaining spot flagged in `packages/types/src/git.ts`'s comments where the pre-existing `/git/repos` response shape includes a raw provider token — noted but not changed in this pass
- `DeploymentsResource.delete()` (part of H10) now fails with a clear error instead of silently 404ing, but there's still no real server-side "delete this deployment record" endpoint — only `stop()`. Adding one needs a deliberate product decision about cascade behavior (subscriptions, invoices, logs) that shouldn't be made unilaterally as part of a bug-fix pass.

None of these were re-verified as still-current in this final pass, and none are urgent.

---

## Before you deploy this

1. **Rotate every secret** that was in the original `apps/api/.env` — especially `NODE_AGENT_SECRET` (C5) and `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (rotating the latter means re-encrypting every existing stored credential — see the original audit's Phase 0 notes).
2. Run `npx prisma migrate deploy` (or generate + review the migrations first) — nine new migrations were added, in order: `20260819000000_settings_pin_hash`, `20260819000100_audit_log_actor_role`, `20260819000200_git_provider_integrations`, `20260819000300_webmail_per_user_scoping`, `20260819000400_knowledgebase_tables`, `20260819000500_smtp_persisted_config`, `20260819000600_email_domain_records`, `20260819000700_secrets_vault_tables`, `20260819000800_supabase_panel_tables`.
3. Set up a real GitHub App and GitLab OAuth application (see the new block in `apps/api/.env.example`) before the "Connect GitHub/GitLab" buttons will do anything — until then, `GET /api/git/config` reports both as unconfigured and the dashboard should hide the buttons accordingly (confirm this UI behavior exists — I didn't add explicit hide-if-unconfigured logic to the button itself in this pass).
4. Every existing user's `settingsPinHash` will be `null` after the migration — the first time anyone tries to unlock Settings, they'll need to set a PIN via `change-pin` first (intentional — see C4).

While implementing it, found and fixed a second, more severe bug: `docker.js` never actually exported `listContainers`/`startContainer`/`getLogs`/`streamLogs` (only destructured as `undefined` in `index.js`), so the Containers page, log viewer, and live log streaming were all crashing with `TypeError` on every real request. All four are now implemented with `dockerode` (including `modem.demuxStream` for live log streaming).
- **C7** — `apps/api/Dockerfile` now `COPY`s `templates/` into the build and runtime stages — the self-hosted app catalog (WordPress/n8n/MongoDB/Redis/Lavalink/LiveKit) was previously always empty in any Docker deployment. Also unified `catalog.ts` and `catalog-manager.ts` onto the same `__dirname`-relative path resolution (previously one used `process.cwd()`, which is fragile to how the process is launched).

## 🟠 High — all fixed except the H1/H8 persistence backlog (see "Not done" below)

- **H2 / H4 (node-agent)** — timing-safe secret comparison (was `!==`); bind host is now configurable (`AGENT_BIND_HOST`, default unchanged at `0.0.0.0` to avoid breaking existing deployments) with an optional `AGENT_ALLOWED_IPS` allowlist and a loud startup warning if neither is set.
- **H3** — Fixed the WhatsApp/Discord bot Docker networking bug: both now bind to all interfaces inside their own container (was `127.0.0.1`, which silently blocks sibling-container access even via Compose service-name DNS) — this was why WhatsApp/Discord notifications were silently never delivered under `docker-compose.local.yml`. Removed the now-pointless host port publishing for both in `docker-compose.local.yml` (they were never meant to be reachable from the host).
- **H4 (vps-plans.ts)** — delete route now matches `products.ts`'s correct pattern: try hard-delete, catch FK-constraint failures, fall back to `isActive: false` instead of a raw 500. (`catalog.ts`'s delete route was re-examined and found to be a different case — it deletes a template *file*, not a DB row with foreign keys, so the same pattern doesn't actually apply there; left as-is.)
- **H5** — Added `redact` config to both the base `pino` logger and the `pino-http` instance — `Authorization`, `x-agent-secret`, `x-internal-secret`, `x-cron-secret`, `x-webhook-secret`, `x-signature` headers, plus common secret-shaped field names, are no longer written to plaintext logs.
- **H6** — Billing sweep and uptime checks now self-schedule via BullMQ in `worker.ts` (daily at 01:00, and every 5 minutes, respectively), matching the pattern SSL renewal already used. No longer dependent on a `.github/workflows/billing-cron.yml` that never existed. The manual "run checks" endpoints in `routes/billing.ts`/`routes/status.ts` still work too.
- **H7 — rewritten as a real feature, not just a bug fix.** Per your follow-up request, the entire Git-connect flow has been replaced:
  - **GitHub**: a real GitHub App integration. Users install the App and pick repos on GitHub's own UI; we store only the installation ID (`GitHubInstallation` model, new migration). Every API call mints a fresh, short-lived (~1hr) installation access token via a signed App JWT — no PAT, no long-lived token stored anywhere.
  - **GitLab**: a real OAuth application integration (`read_user read_repository` scopes only). Access + refresh tokens are encrypted at rest (`GitLabConnection` model, same migration) and refreshed automatically when expired.
  - Both sit behind a common `GitProviderAdapter` interface (`lib/gitProviders/types.ts`) so a third provider is "implement the interface, register it in `index.ts`" — nothing else changes.
  - A signed, single-use, 5-minute `state` parameter replaces the old raw-user-ID state (fixes the account-linking CSRF weakness).
  - The dashboard's "Connect GitHub/GitLab" now redirects the browser directly to the provider — there is no token-paste modal or input field anywhere in the flow anymore.
  - `routes/deployments.ts` and `routes/filesystem.ts`'s git-push both resolve a scoped token server-side from a connected account ID; `gitToken` is retained only for `gitProvider: 'custom'` (self-hosted git hosts with no App/OAuth integration here).
- **H8** — Solved as a side effect of the H7 rewrite: the old unpersisted, in-memory `gitUserAccounts` map is gone entirely, replaced by the two real, persisted Prisma models above.
- **H9** — Added audit logging to `leaseweb.ts`'s `credentials` and `ssh-ticket` routes (previously the two most sensitive actions in that file left no trail at all). Added a new nullable `AuditLog.actorRole` column (migration `20260819000100_audit_log_actor_role`) so customer self-service actions (like VPS password reset) are distinguishable from genuine staff actions — populated on all three routes now.
- **H10** — Fixed every broken SDK path/shape found in the original audit:
  - `packages/node-agent`: `stopContainer`/`startContainer`/`restartContainer` now call the real `/agent/deployments/:id/{action}` routes.
  - `packages/client`'s `deployments.ts`: `getResourceUsage` now reads from the real detail response instead of a nonexistent `/stats` route; `addDomain`/`removeDomain` now hit the real `/custom-domain` route with the right shape (plus a new `verifyDomain()`); `delete()` now throws a clear, explicit error instead of silently 404ing, since there genuinely is no server-side delete-the-record route (that's a product decision outside the scope of a bug fix — see "Not done" below).
  - `packages/client`'s `git.ts`: rewritten entirely to match the new H7 architecture — `removeAccount` now uses the real `/git/disconnect` endpoint; `resolveAccountForRepo`'s broken `.login` property lookup fixed (`packages/types`' `GitAccount`/`GitRepo` types corrected to match what the API actually returns).

## 🟡 Medium — all fixed

- **M1** — Replaced the reflect-any-Origin-with-credentials CORS middleware with the `cors` package configured against an explicit allowlist (the same one `csrfProtection.ts` already maintained — now shared via `isOriginAllowed()` instead of being duplicated).
- **M2/M3** — `.env.example` updated: documented that `WHATSAPP_BOT_URL`/`DISCORD_BOT_URL` need Compose service names under Docker (not `localhost`), and added the new GitHub App / GitLab OAuth variables.
- **M6** — `billing.ts`'s cron-fallback now allows `dev` role, not just `admin`, matching `requireAdmin`'s behavior everywhere else.
- **M7** — Deleted `lib/verifyPayment.ts.disabled`, `lib/gemini.ts`, `lib/groq.ts` (confirmed dead — nothing imported them) and their now-unused `GEMINI_API_KEY`/`GROQ_API_KEY` env vars.
- **M8** — Fixed the double-mounted `settingsRouter` (was mounted at both `/api/settings` and `/api`, with route paths that happened to paper over it). Now mounted once at `/api/settings` with route paths matching exactly what the dashboard frontend already calls (`verify-password`, `change-pin`, `configs`).

## Templates: hardcoded default passwords — fully fixed, including auto-generation

All six `templates/*.yaml` files (WordPress, n8n, MongoDB, Redis, Lavalink, LiveKit) had weak, now-public default passwords baked in via Compose's `${VAR:-default}` fallback syntax. These have been changed to `${VAR:?VAR must be set}` (Compose's required-variable syntax — fails loudly instead of silently deploying with a known weak password).

`routes/catalog.ts`'s deploy handler now auto-generates a strong random value (`crypto.randomBytes(24).toString('base64url')`) for each of these specific keys whenever the customer doesn't supply one, so a deploy never actually fails because of this — and returns the generated values in the deploy response (`generatedSecrets`) so the customer can save them. This was the piece flagged as incomplete in the previous version of this changelog; it's now done.

## C3 — webmail cross-tenant IDOR — fixed

`routes/webmail.ts` is now backed by a real, per-user-owned `WebmailMessage` Prisma model (migration `20260819000300_webmail_per_user_scoping`) instead of a single global in-memory `Map` shared by every user on the platform. Every route (`list`, `get`, `patch`, `delete`) filters by the authenticated user's own ID — a message belonging to another user simply doesn't match the query and 404s, closing the IDOR.

As part of the same fix, `POST /webmail/send` now sends through the user's actual provisioned `SmtpAccount` credentials (same `encryptSecret`/`decryptSecret` pattern already used correctly in `routes/smtp.ts`/`routes/email.ts`) instead of the old undocumented `SMTP_HOST`/`SMTP_USER`/`SMTP_PASS` env vars with a hardcoded fallback password — this also resolves M4/M5 from the original audit. Delivery failures are now awaited and surfaced to the caller (`502` with the saved draft still returned) instead of silently disappearing into an unawaited background promise.

## H1 — every remaining in-memory store persisted

All four remaining unpersisted, in-memory feature stores identified in the original audit have now been replaced with real Prisma-backed tables, following the same pattern established by the git-provider and webmail rewrites above:

- **Knowledge Base** (`routes/knowledgebase.ts`) — new `KbArticle`/`KbCategory` models (migration `20260819000400_knowledgebase_tables`, seeded with the original demo content so behavior is unchanged immediately after migrating). All CRUD routes rewritten.
- **Global SMTP config + per-account domains/aliases** (`routes/smtp.ts`) — the platform-wide outbound mail config is now a persisted `PlatformSmtpConfig` singleton (password encrypted via `secretsVault`, migration `20260819000500_smtp_persisted_config`); per-account custom domain + alias list now live directly on `SmtpAccount` (new columns in the same migration). The hardcoded fallback password (`'smtp_secret_pass'`) is now only used to seed the config row the very first time it's read, not as a permanent runtime fallback.
- **Custom email domain verification records** (`routes/email.ts`) — new `EmailDomain` model (migration `20260819000600_email_domain_records`).
- **Secrets Vault** (`routes/secrets.ts`) — new `SecretProject`/`SecretItem`/`SecretAuditEntry` models (migration `20260819000700_secrets_vault_tables`). Secret values are now actually encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM via the existing `secretsVault`) — the previous in-memory version stored them as plaintext despite being branded a "vault."
- **Supabase management panel** (`routes/supabase.ts`) — new `SupabaseClientProject`, `SupabaseAuthSmtpConfig`, `SupabaseEmailTemplate`, `SupabaseSmtpDeliveryLog` models (migration `20260819000800_supabase_panel_tables`, seeded with the original demo content/templates). **Scope note:** this only fixes the persistence bug — it does not make the "client projects" into real, separately-provisioned, isolated Supabase stacks (this platform runs one shared Kong/GoTrue/PostgREST stack under the hood). That's a genuine infrastructure project, not a bug fix, and is out of scope here.

All dashboard-facing response shapes were preserved exactly (verified against `lib/api.ts` and `lib/secretsApi.ts`), so no frontend changes were needed for any of these five.

---

## Everything from the original audit is now addressed

Every Critical, High, and Medium finding from the original audit report — including every item raised across all follow-up review passes — has been fixed. What's left is only the "Low / cleanup" tier from the very first version of the audit report:

- The 40 Prisma relations without an explicit `onDelete` (likely intentional, given the soft-delete pattern used elsewhere — worth a confirmation pass, not an urgent fix)
- `CLAUDE.md` claims Next.js 15; the actual pinned version is 14.2.35
- One remaining spot flagged in `packages/types/src/git.ts`'s comments where the pre-existing `/git/repos` response shape includes a raw provider token — noted but not changed in this pass
- `DeploymentsResource.delete()` (part of H10) now fails with a clear error instead of silently 404ing, but there's still no real server-side "delete this deployment record" endpoint — only `stop()`. Adding one needs a deliberate product decision about cascade behavior (subscriptions, invoices, logs) that shouldn't be made unilaterally as part of a bug-fix pass.

None of these were re-verified as still-current in this final pass, and none are urgent.

---

## Before you deploy this

1. **Rotate every secret** that was in the original `apps/api/.env` — especially `NODE_AGENT_SECRET` (C5) and `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (rotating the latter means re-encrypting every existing stored credential — see the original audit's Phase 0 notes).
2. Run `npx prisma migrate deploy` (or generate + review the migrations first) — nine new migrations were added, in order: `20260819000000_settings_pin_hash`, `20260819000100_audit_log_actor_role`, `20260819000200_git_provider_integrations`, `20260819000300_webmail_per_user_scoping`, `20260819000400_knowledgebase_tables`, `20260819000500_smtp_persisted_config`, `20260819000600_email_domain_records`, `20260819000700_secrets_vault_tables`, `20260819000800_supabase_panel_tables`.
3. Set up a real GitHub App and GitLab OAuth application (see the new block in `apps/api/.env.example`) before the "Connect GitHub/GitLab" buttons will do anything — until then, `GET /api/git/config` reports both as unconfigured and the dashboard should hide the buttons accordingly (confirm this UI behavior exists — I didn't add explicit hide-if-unconfigured logic to the button itself in this pass).
4. Every existing user's `settingsPinHash` will be `null` after the migration — the first time anyone tries to unlock Settings, they'll need to set a PIN via `change-pin` first (intentional — see C4).

# Working notes (raw, will be organized into final report)

## apps/api/src/routes/deployments.ts

1. [MEDIUM] Inconsistent admin visibility: `GET /deployments` (list) uses `ownedResourceWhere()` 
   which for admin = ONLY customers with `assignedAdminId === admin.id`. But every detail/action route
   (`loadOwnedDeployment` -> `canAccessResource`) uses assignedAdminId === admin.id OR assignedAdminId == null (unassigned).
   Result: an admin can GET/stop/start/delete/redeploy a specific deployment belonging to an UNASSIGNED
   customer by ID even though it never appears in their list. Likely unintended inconsistency between
   rbac.ts's `ownedResourceWhere` (strict) and `canAccessResource`/`verifyResourceOwnershipAsync` (loose,
   includes unassigned). File: middleware/rbac.ts (lines ~256-271 vs ~138-149), used from routes/deployments.ts,
   routes/vps.ts, routes/invoices.ts, routes/domains.ts, routes/smtp.ts, routes/email.ts, routes/leaseweb.ts,
   routes/managedDatabases.ts, routes/livekit.ts, routes/apiKeys.ts, routes/billing.ts, routes/cockpit.ts,
   routes/deployWebhooks.ts, routes/filesystem.ts, routes/orders.ts -- need to check each of these too.

2. [MEDIUM] PATCH /deployments/:id/subdomain: creates a NEW Cloudflare DNS record for the new subdomain
   via createSubdomainRecord(), but never deletes/cleans up the OLD subdomain's DNS record. Old CNAME
   for the previous subdomain is orphaned indefinitely (resource leak / stale DNS pointing at the node).

3. [MEDIUM-HIGH] PATCH /deployments/:id/limits: on buildAndRun failure (result.phase==='error'), writes
   an ndjson error event but does NOT set deployment.status to 'failed' in DB (contrast with /redeploy
   and /env which both do `prisma.deployment.update(... status:'failed')` on the same failure path).
   DB can be left saying status:'running' while the container actually failed to restart with new limits.
   Also this endpoint does not call stopDeployment() before buildAndRun (unlike /env which does
   `await stopDeployment(...)` first) -- need to check buildAndRun/nodeAgentClient to see if it's
   idempotent/self-stopping; if not, could leave orphaned container or port conflict. TO VERIFY.

4. [LOW] /deployments/:id/preview: `parsed.data.branch` used in `preferredName` template string --
   this becomes part of container/subdomain naming presumably; branch already regex-validated so ok.
EOF
echo done

## CONFIRMED CRITICAL: resource limits (cpuLimit/memoryLimit/storageLimit) never applied by node-agent

File: services/node-agent/src/index.js, POST /agent/deployments/:deploymentId/build-and-run (~line 165)
```
const { repoUrl, branch, subdomain, internalPort, envVars } = req.body || {};
...
const { containerId, containerName } = await runContainer({
  deploymentId, imageTag, internalPort, subdomain, rootDomain: ROOT_DOMAIN, envVars,
});
```
`runContainer()` (services/node-agent/src/docker.js) accepts `cpuLimit`, `memLimitMb`, `routingMode`,
`publishedPort` and defaults them to `cpuLimit = 1`, `memLimitMb = 512`, `routingMode = 'proxied'` when
not passed. But the build-and-run route NEVER destructures/forwards cpuLimit/memoryLimit/storageLimit (or
routingMode/publishedPort) from req.body to runContainer(). 

apps/api's lib/nodeAgentClient.ts `BuildAndRunParams` interface DOES include cpuLimit/memoryLimit/storageLimit
and apps/api DOES send them (JSON.stringify(params) includes them) from multiple call sites:
- routes/deployments.ts PATCH /deployments/:id/limits (the entire point of this endpoint is to change
  cpu/memory/storage limits and restart the container to "apply" them -- comment literally says
  "The deployment is restarted automatically to ensure the new limits are enforced by Docker")
- routes/deployments.ts POST /deployments (initial deploy also passes cpuLimit/memoryLimit/storageLimit
  -- need to check deployPipeline.ts/buildAndRun call there too)
- routes/deployments.ts PATCH /deployments/:id/env (passes cpuLimit/memoryLimit/storageLimit through on env update restart)

Net effect: every container ever created by this platform runs with the hardcoded default 1 CPU / 512MB
memory limit, REGARDLESS of what plan/limits the customer purchased or what admin/dev explicitly set via
the resource-limits endpoint. The PATCH /deployments/:id/limits feature is completely non-functional --
it updates the DB row (deployment.cpuLimit/memoryLimit/storageLimit) and shows a success message, but the
actual container is silently deployed with defaults every single time. This is a billing/plan-enforcement
integrity bug (customers on higher-tier plans get no more resources than free-tier customers) as well as
a straightforward "feature doesn't work" bug.

Severity: CRITICAL (silent, no error, billing/plan integrity + resource isolation impact).
EOF
echo done

cat >> /home/claude/notes/findings.md << 'EOF'

## CONFIRMED CRITICAL: "Stop" force-removes the container, so "Start" always fails afterward

Files: 
- services/node-agent/src/index.js: `POST /agent/deployments/:containerId/stop` calls `stopAndRemove(containerId)`
- services/node-agent/src/docker.js: `stopAndRemove` = `container.remove({ force: true })` -- this DELETES the
  container from the node's Docker daemon entirely (not merely stopping it). Contrast with `stopContainer`
  (also in docker.js, used only by the separate raw `/agent/containers/:id/stop` admin route) which does a
  plain `container.stop()` with no removal.
- apps/api/src/routes/deployments.ts: `POST /deployments/:id/stop` calls `stopDeployment()` (-> the
  stopAndRemove-backed route above), sets `deployment.status = 'stopped'` in the DB, but never clears
  `deployment.containerId`.
- apps/api/src/routes/deployments.ts: `POST /deployments/:id/start` calls `startDeployment()`
  (-> node-agent's `/agent/deployments/:containerId/start` -> `docker.getContainer(containerId).start()`)
  using that same now-stale containerId.
- apps/dashboard/app/(protected)/deployments/[id]/page.tsx confirms the UI actually offers a "Start"
  button whenever `deployment.status === 'stopped' || deployment.status === 'failed'`, calling
  `api.deployments.start(deploymentId)`.

Why it's a bug: once a deployment is stopped, its container no longer exists on the node (Docker returns
404 for that ID). The very next "Start" attempt therefore always fails at the Docker API layer, is caught
by node-agent, returned as a 500, translated by apps/api into a 502 "Failed to start deployment on node".
There is no code path that clears/recreates containerId after stop, so the customer-facing Start button is
permanently broken for any deployment that has ever been stopped -- the only way to bring it back is
`/deployments/:id/redeploy`, which rebuilds from scratch via `runContainer`'s name-based
`removeContainerIfExists` (works because it doesn't depend on the old ID). This is a confirmed, easily
reproducible functional/UX bug with no error recovery in the UI beyond a generic failure toast.

Severity: CRITICAL (core lifecycle feature broken for every deployment on the platform).
Suggested fix: either (a) make `/agent/deployments/:id/stop` a plain stop (no remove), matching the
`/agent/containers/:id/stop` semantics, and have `/start` truly restart the same container; or (b) if
force-remove-on-stop is intentional (e.g. to free node resources), have the api-level `/start` route
detect a missing container and transparently redeploy/rebuild instead of calling the now-defunct
containerId, and update the UI/copy accordingly.
EOF
echo done

input.command:
cat >> /home/claude/notes/findings.md << 'EOF'

## CONFIRMED CRITICAL: Project Table Editor insert/update/delete row endpoints don't exist on node-agent (404s)

Files: 
- apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts: `POST /projects/:id/tables/:table/rows`, `PATCH .../rows/:pk`,
  `DELETE .../rows/:pk` all proxy (via `proxyToAgent`) to node-agent paths
  `POST/PATCH/DELETE /agent/projects/:projectId/tables/:table/rows[/:pk]`.
- services/node-agent/src/index.js: only `GET /agent/projects/:projectId/tables` and
  `GET /agent/projects/:projectId/tables/:table/rows` are implemented. There is NO
  POST/PATCH/DELETE route under `/agent/projects/:projectId/tables/...` anywhere in the file (confirmed
  via grep across all `app.get|post|patch|delete` registrations).
- apps/dashboard/lib/api.ts (`insertRow`, `updateRow`, `deleteRow`) and
  apps/dashboard/app/(protected)/projects/[id]/page.tsx wire real "Add row" / "Edit row" / "Delete row"
  buttons in the Table Editor UI to these same three apps/api endpoints.

Why it's a bug: any insert/update/delete attempt from the Table Editor hits apps/api's `proxyToAgent`,
which fetches a node-agent URL that doesn't exist, so Express's default handler returns a 404 (HTML, not
JSON). `proxyToAgent` does `agentRes.json().catch(() => ({}))`, silently swallowing the JSON-parse failure
and returning `res.status(404).json({})` to the dashboard -- an empty-object 404 with no useful error
message. The entire write path of the Table Editor feature (the primary way to manage data in a
dev-provisioned Project's database through the UI, short of writing raw SQL) is completely non-functional.
Only read (GET rows, GET tables) works.

Severity: CRITICAL for the feature (100% broken, silently, for every project). Actual customer-facing
impact is limited to the `dev` role (this whole router requires `requireDev`), so it doesn't affect paying
customers directly, but it does mean the "self-hosted Supabase-like" project data management UI is
unusable for its main purpose.

Suggested fix: implement the three missing node-agent routes (translate to parameterized INSERT/UPDATE/
DELETE via psql, validating `table` with the existing `validateIdentifier` helper from projects.js first).

## MEDIUM: SQL injection via unvalidated `:table` route param in GET /agent/projects/:projectId/tables/:table/rows

File: services/node-agent/src/index.js (~line 718-732)
```js
app.get('/agent/projects/:projectId/tables/:table/rows', async (req, res) => {
  ...
  sql: `SELECT * FROM "${req.params.table}" LIMIT ${parseInt(limit)} OFFSET ${offset};`
  ...
  sql: `SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM "${req.params.table}";`
```
`req.params.table` is taken directly from the URL and interpolated into a double-quoted SQL identifier
with no call to `validateIdentifier()` (which projects.js already defines and correctly uses inside
`listTables()` for the same purpose) and no escaping of embedded `"` characters. A crafted `table` value
containing a `"` can break out of the identifier and inject arbitrary additional SQL, which `psql` (invoked
via stdin, not a parameterized driver) will execute as a multi-statement script.

Mitigating factor: this route (and the whole `apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts` router it's reached
through) requires the `dev` platform role (`requireDev`), and `dev` already has an intentional raw-SQL
execution endpoint (`POST /projects/:id/sql`) against the exact same database connection/role, so this
doesn't grant a *new* privilege to that actor -- it's an inconsistency/defense-in-depth gap rather than a
privilege escalation. Still worth fixing for consistency (`listTables` in the same file already validates
identifiers the same way) and in case this route is ever exposed to a less-trusted role in the future.

Severity: MEDIUM (real injection, but reachable only by the already-fully-trusted `dev` role).
EOF
echo done

input.command:
cat >> /home/claude/notes/findings.md << 'EOF'

## HIGH (latent, currently masked by another bug): shadow-backup restore path never wired up -> permanent data loss risk for zip/upload deployments after workspace cleanup

Files: services/node-agent/src/repo.js (`prepareWorkspace`), services/node-agent/src/index.js
(`POST /agent/deployments/:deploymentId/build-and-run`), apps/api/src/lib/nodeAgentClient.ts
(`BuildAndRunParams`).

`prepareWorkspace(deploymentId, repoUrl, branch, remoteBackupUrl)` has a documented "Pull-to-Restore"
path: if the local workspace dir is empty (e.g. purged by the 24h retention job) AND `remoteBackupUrl` is
given, it git-clones from the shadow backup repo before falling back to normal handling. But:
- The only real caller, `build-and-run` in index.js, calls `prepareWorkspace(deploymentId, repoUrl, branch || 'main')`
  -- only 3 args, so `remoteBackupUrl` is always `undefined`.
- `BuildAndRunParams` (nodeAgentClient.ts) and every apps/api call site that builds this payload
  (deployPipeline.ts, routes/deployments.ts redeploy/limits/env handlers) has no `remoteBackupUrl`/backup
  URL field at all -- there is no plumbing anywhere from the Deployment's shadow-backup repo URL
  (see lib/shadowBackup.ts) into a build-and-run request.
- For non-Git deployments specifically (`repoUrl` starting with `zip://` or `upload://` -- exactly the
  ones the workspace-cleanup job targets), `prepareWorkspace` has no other way to reconstruct the source:
  the `zip://`/`upload://` branch (line 47-49) just returns the (now-empty) directory as-is.

Net effect: if a zip/manual-upload deployment's node workspace is ever purged by the 24h retention job (see
the separate cleanup-route bug above -- today it's masked because that job always fails, so nothing is
actually purged yet), the next `/redeploy` or restart-triggering action (env var update, resource limit

I was about two hours into a genuinely full-repo audit (I'd scoped it down to ~458 first-party source files, ~64K LOC, after confirming `packages/{auth-js,postgrest-js,realtime-js,functions-js,storage-js,supabase-js}` are vendored 1:1 forks of the real Supabase SDK repos and excluding them per your instructions). Here's what I confirmed before running out of calls, in case it's useful now — I'd need another turn to finish the sweep and write the actual report file.

**Critical**
1. **Resource limits are never applied to containers.** `services/node-agent/src/index.js`'s `build-and-run` route never forwards `cpuLimit`/`memoryLimit`/`storageLimit` from the request body to `runContainer()`, even though `docker.js` supports them and apps/api sends them on every deploy/redeploy/limit-update. Every container silently runs at the hardcoded default (1 CPU / 512MB), regardless of plan or explicit admin override — `PATCH /deployments/:id/limits` updates the DB and reports success but changes nothing real.
2. **"Stop" permanently breaks "Start."** The deployment-level stop route calls `stopAndRemove()` (force-removes the container), but `containerId` is never cleared, and `/start` tries to start that same now-deleted container ID. Confirmed the dashboard actually offers a Start button whenever status is `stopped`/`failed`. Every stop→start cycle 502s.
3. **Table Editor writes are 100% broken.** `apps/api/routes/projects.ts` proxies insert/update/delete row requests to node-agent routes that were never implemented (`grep` across all `app.post/patch/delete` in node-agent's `index.js` confirms only GET exists). Dashboard wires real Add/Edit/Delete buttons to this dead path; all silently 404.

**High**
4. Node-agent's workspace-cleanup route references `path`/`fs` that are never `require()`d in that file — always throws, always fails, so 24h workspace retention never actually purges anything (disk leak on every node).
5. The shadow-backup "restore after cleanup" path in `repo.js` requires a `remoteBackupUrl` parameter that no caller ever supplies — latent data-loss bug, currently masked by bug #4 but would activate the moment that one's fixed.

**Medium**
6. SQL injection via unvalidated `:table` route param in one node-agent route (missing the `validateIdentifier()` call used elsewhere in the same file) — real, but only reachable by the already-fully-trusted `dev` role.
7. Inconsistent admin visibility rules: `ownedResourceWhere()` (list endpoints) excludes unassigned customers' resources for admin, but `canAccessResource()`/`verifyResourceOwnershipAsync()` (detail/action endpoints) include them — an admin can act on a specific unassigned-customer resource by ID that never shows up in their own list view. Affects ~14 route files.
8. `PATCH /deployments/:id/subdomain` creates a new Cloudflare CNAME but never deletes the old one (orphaned DNS record).
9. `PATCH /deployments/:id/limits` doesn't mark the deployment `status: 'failed'` on a failed restart (unlike the sibling `/redeploy` and `/env` routes), leaving the DB claiming "running" when the container actually failed.

## CONFIRMED HIGH: cockpit.ts uses VpsProvision.externalId (an opaque provider instance ID) as if it were an IP address

File: apps/api/src/routes/cockpit.ts, `resolveNodeAccess()` (~line 22-45)
```js
const provision = await prisma.vpsProvision.findUnique({ where: { id: nodeId } });
if (provision) {
  const allowed = await canAccessResource(provision.userId, req);
  if (!allowed) return null;
  return {
    id: provision.id,
    label: `vps-${provision.externalId || provision.id.slice(0, 8)}`,
    ip: provision.externalId || '127.0.0.1',   // <-- BUG
  };
}
```
`VpsProvision.externalId` is documented in the Prisma schema as *"the upstream provider's VPS/instance
ID"* (packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma ~line 618) -- an opaque identifier like a Leaseweb server ID, not
an IP address. Every other place in the codebase that needs a VPS's real IP resolves it dynamically from
the provider API (see routes/leaseweb.ts ~line 147: `const ip = vpsInfo.ips?.[0]?.ip;`), precisely because
the IP isn't stored directly on the model.

Every Cockpit route (`/nodes/:nodeId/cockpit/monitoring|services|users|docker/containers|firewall|ssh-ticket`)
routes through `resolveNodeAccess`, so for any customer-owned VPS provision (as opposed to a cluster Node),
the constructed `agentUrl(node.ip, ...)` will either:
  - be built from a non-IP string (e.g. a Leaseweb instance ID like `12345678`), which is not a valid
    hostname/IP and will fail DNS/connect immediately, so Cockpit management is completely non-functional
    for every customer VPS; or
  - if `externalId` happens to be null/empty, silently fall back to `'127.0.0.1'` -- i.e. the API server's
    own loopback. In any deployment topology where the API and a node-agent (or any other service bound to
    localhost) run on the same host, this would direct systemd/user-management/Docker/firewall commands at
    the wrong target instead of failing loudly, which is a much worse outcome than a clean error.

Severity: HIGH (feature completely broken for its stated purpose; the `127.0.0.1` fallback branch is a
latent wrong-target risk in colocated deployments).
Suggested fix: resolve the real IP the same way leaseweb.ts does (via the Leaseweb API using
`provision.leasewebVpsId`), and drop the `'127.0.0.1'` fallback in favor of a clear error when the IP
can't be resolved.
EOF
echo done

input.command:
cat >> /home/claude/notes/findings.md << 'EOF'

## MEDIUM-HIGH: race condition -- Deployment.subdomain has no unique DB constraint, but uniqueness is only enforced by a check-then-act app-level query

File: apps/api/src/lib/subdomain.ts (`generateSubdomain`/`isTaken`/`validateCustomSubdomain`),
packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma (`Deployment.subdomain String?` -- confirmed NO `@unique` attribute,
grepped the whole schema).

`generateSubdomain()` loops `isTaken(candidate)` (a `findFirst` query) until it finds a free name, then
returns it; the caller (`deployPipeline.ts`) creates the Deployment row afterward, and separately calls
`createSubdomainRecord()` (Cloudflare DNS) using that name. There is no unique index, transaction, or
advisory lock covering the check-then-create window. Two concurrent deploy requests that independently
compute the same candidate subdomain (same repo/app name is common -- e.g. two different customers both
naming their app "api", or a user double-submitting the deploy form) can both pass `isTaken` before either
`Deployment` row exists, producing two deployments with the identical `subdomain` value. Since Traefik
routing (`docker.js`'s `Host(...)` label) and Cloudflare DNS are keyed by subdomain, this causes two
containers competing for the same hostname/route and a duplicate/conflicting DNS record creation. The same
race applies to `PATCH /deployments/:id/subdomain` via `validateCustomSubdomain`.

Severity: MEDIUM-HIGH (low-probability but real race; no DB constraint as a backstop, so a collision that
does occur isn't just rejected at write time -- it silently succeeds and produces two live deployments
sharing one hostname).
Suggested fix: add `@unique` to `Deployment.subdomain` in the Prisma schema and handle the resulting
P2002 error with a retry/regenerate, instead of (or in addition to) the pre-check.
EOF
echo done

worth flagging since the name and docstring strongly imply working automatic failover that does not
exist).

9. Cockpit SSH terminal always fails to authenticate for any node registered without an explicit private key (comment claims a fallback that was never implemented).

summaries.summary: Validated code pathway and fallback behavior mechanism.

input.command:
cat >> /home/claude/notes/findings.md << 'EOF'

## CONFIRMED MEDIUM-HIGH: Cockpit SSH terminal always fails to authenticate for nodes registered without an explicit private key

Files: apps/api/src/routes/nodes.ts (~lines 436-438, 557-558), apps/api/src/lib/sshTerminalGateway.ts
(~lines 145-161).

When an admin registers/re-probes a Node without supplying `privateKey` in the request, `nodes.ts` stores
`sshKeyRef = \`ssh://${username}@${ip}:${port}\`` literally (unencrypted placeholder string) instead of an
encrypted private key blob. `sshTerminalGateway.ts`'s `node:` connection branch detects this format
(`sshKeyRef.startsWith('ssh://')`) and its own comment says: *"password SSH requires re-prompting (not
supported in this flow). Use key auth."* -- but the code in that branch only sets `connectOpts.username`;
it never sets `connectOpts.password` or `connectOpts.privateKey`. `ssh2`'s `.connect(connectOpts)` is then
called with no authentication method configured at all, which always fails
("All configured authentication methods failed") and surfaces to the user as a generic
"SSH connection failed" message.

Net effect: the Cockpit browser-terminal feature is guaranteed to be broken for every Node that was added
to the cluster without explicitly supplying an SSH private key at registration time -- a very plausible
real-world case (e.g. an admin bootstrapping a node with password auth, planning to add the key later, or
simply not realizing the field is required for this feature to work).

Severity: MEDIUM-HIGH (real, reachable, silent-until-used feature break with no code path that could ever
make it work as written -- there's no re-prompt-for-password flow anywhere in the WS handshake).
EOF
echo done

Investigated duplicate execution risks across multiple call sites.

input.command:
cat >> /home/claude/notes/findings.md << 'EOF'

## HIGH: SMTP mailbox passwords generated with Math.random() plus a hardcoded, identical suffix for every account

File: apps/api/src/lib/orderFulfillment.ts (~line 94)
```js
const autoPassword = `Smtp_${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10)}!2026`;
```
Two separate problems, both confirmed by reading the surrounding code:
1. `Math.random()` is not a cryptographically secure random source (V8's PRNG is not designed to resist
   prediction) -- compare with the Managed Database block 90 lines below in the very same file, which
   correctly uses `crypto.randomBytes(16).toString('hex')` for its auto-generated password. The
   inconsistency confirms this isn't a deliberate simplicity trade-off elsewhere in the codebase.
2. Every single auto-provisioned SMTP mailbox password ends in the literal, identical, hardcoded string
   `!2026` -- almost certainly added only to satisfy a "must contain a digit and special character"
   complexity rule, but doing so with a fixed, non-random suffix means part of every customer's mailbox
   password is knowable in advance to anyone who has seen this source file (as this audit has), and it
   shrinks the effective brute-force search space to just the random prefix.

Severity: HIGH (real, live credential-generation weakness affecting every automatically-provisioned SMTP
account on the platform).
Suggested fix: `crypto.randomBytes(n).toString('base64url')` (or similar), no fixed suffix.

## MEDIUM-HIGH: Managed Database auto-provisioning has no idempotency guard (unlike SMTP/LiveKit in the same function) and ignores node health/role tags

File: apps/api/src/lib/orderFulfillment.ts, Managed Database block (~lines 176-215)
- No `prisma.managedDatabase.findFirst({ where: { orderItemId: item.id }})` existence check before
  creating a new `ManagedDatabase` row + container, unlike the SMTP block (`existingAccount` check,
  ~line 87) and the LiveKit block (`existingLk` check, ~line 142) directly above it in the same function.
  If `fulfillOrder()` is ever invoked twice for the same order (all three call sites --
  routes/payments.ts, routes/orders.ts, routes/internalBot.ts -- would need to be individually verified
  for their own dedup guards, but nothing in `orderFulfillment.ts` itself prevents it), the customer ends
  up with duplicate database containers silently provisioned and billed against cluster capacity for one
  purchased item.
- `const node = await prisma.node.findFirst();` picks whatever row Postgres returns first with NO
  filtering on `isActive`, no role-tag check (contrast with the platform's own `selectNodeForDeployment()`
  helper, used correctly for LiveKit's primary path just above), and no capacity/headroom weighting. Every
  managed database on the entire platform can land on the same single node regardless of whether that node
  is intended/tagged for database hosting, is currently active, or has any free capacity -- and if that
  node happens to be inactive, provisioning silently fails (falls into the `.catch` -> `status: 'failed'`
  branch) with no specific diagnostic.
Severity: MEDIUM-HIGH (duplicate-resource risk + poor/incorrect node placement for a billed customer
resource).
EOF
echo done

summaries.summary: Identified multiple security vulnerabilities in file upload authorization logic.

input.command:
cat >> /home/claude/notes/findings.md << 'EOF'

## MEDIUM: Payment-proof upload writes to disk (keyed by raw, unvalidated :orderId) before ownership is checked

Files: apps/api/src/lib/uploads.ts (`multer.diskStorage.destination`), apps/api/src/routes/payments.ts
(`POST /orders/:orderId/payments/proof`, ~lines 38-56).

`uploadPaymentProof(req, res, cb)` is invoked as the very first thing in the handler, and multer's
`destination` callback builds the target directory as
`path.join(UPLOADS_DIR, 'payments', req.params.orderId)` and creates it with `mkdir(..., {recursive:true})`,
using the raw route param straight from the URL -- with no format check (e.g. a CUID regex) and no
ownership check. `loadOwnedOrder(req, req.params.orderId)` (the actual ownership/authorization check) only
runs *after* multer has already written the file to disk, and only gates whether a `Payment` DB row gets
created / a success response is returned.

Two consequences, both real given the current code:
1. Any authenticated user can cause a file to be written into `payments/<any orderId>/`, including order
   IDs belonging to other customers -- the request will ultimately 404 (no Payment row created, since
   ownership fails), but the uploaded file is left orphaned on disk in that other customer's proof folder
   with no cleanup, and no record of who put it there.
2. Because `:orderId` isn't validated as a well-formed CUID before being interpolated into `path.join`,
   this is also a mild path-traversal surface: a crafted `orderId` segment (e.g. containing `..`) could
   cause `path.join` to resolve outside the intended `payments/` subtree. (Express's default router
   collapses `/` inside a single `:param` segment, limiting -- but depending on proxy/normalization
   behavior in front of the app, not fully eliminating -- how much traversal is reachable this way; flagged
   as the concrete, confirmed part is the missing ownership-before-write ordering, with traversal as a
   secondary, environment-dependent risk worth checking directly.)

Severity: MEDIUM (authorization check happens after the side effect it's meant to gate; disk pollution
across tenants; path-traversal risk needs runtime verification against the actual reverse-proxy/Express
config).
Suggested fix: validate `req.params.orderId` against a strict ID pattern and confirm ownership (a cheap
`prisma.order.findUnique` for existence+ownership) *before* invoking `uploadPaymentProof`, not after.
EOF
echo done

## CONFIRMED CRITICAL (likely the single worst finding): Managed-database backup/restore is entirely fake -- customers get a fabricated "success" while no real backup or restore ever happens

Files: apps/api/src/lib/managedDbBackup.ts (`createManagedDatabaseBackup`, `restoreManagedDatabaseBackup`),
apps/api/src/routes/managedDatabases.ts (`POST /managed-databases/:id/backups`,
`POST /managed-databases/:id/restore` -- gated only by `canAccessResource(db.userId, req)`, i.e. this is a
customer-facing feature, not admin/dev-only).

**Backup (`createManagedDatabaseBackup`)**:
```js
const password = db.credentialRef ? decryptSecret(db.credentialRef, env.secretsEncryptionKey) : '';
// Execute real database dump binary stream   <-- comment claims this, but:
const { runBackup } = await import('./backup');
const backupResult = await runBackup().catch(() => ({ key, sizeBytes: 1024 }));
...
const dumpContent = Buffer.from(`-- Backup dump for database ${db.id} (${db.type})\n-- Created at: ${timestamp}\n`);
await client.send(new PutObjectCommand({ ..., Body: dumpContent, ... }));
```
Three independent, compounding problems:
1. `runBackup()` is imported from `lib/backup.ts` -- that function dumps the **platform's own
   control-plane Postgres database** (`env.databaseUrl`), completely unrelated to the customer's managed
   database (`db.node`, `db.type`, the just-decrypted `password` -- none of which are ever passed to
   `runBackup()` or used for anything). Calling this "backs up" the wrong database entirely.
2. Whatever `runBackup()` returns is then **discarded** -- the actual object uploaded to R2
   (`dumpContent`) is a hardcoded, ~90-byte placeholder text comment, not real dumped data of any kind.
   Every "backup" ever created by this endpoint is functionally empty.
3. If `runBackup()` throws (e.g. because it's dumping a database with different credentials/availability
   than expected, or `pg_dump` fails for any reason), the `.catch(() => ({ key, sizeBytes: 1024 }))`
   swallows the error completely and fabricates a fake successful-looking result (`sizeBytes: 1024`), so
   even total dump failure is reported to the customer as a successful backup with a plausible non-zero
   size.

**Restore (`restoreManagedDatabaseBackup`)**:
```js

  const db = await prisma.managedDatabase.findUnique({ where: { id: databaseId } });
  if (!db) throw new Error(...);
  logger.info({ databaseId, backupKey }, 'Managed database restore initiated');
  return { success: true };
}
```
This does not fetch anything from R2, does not run any restore command, and does not touch the actual
database container in any way. It unconditionally returns `{ success: true }` after only logging a line.

Why it's critical: this is presented to customers as a working backup/restore feature

the moment of the actual incident -- that there was never any real backup to restore, with zero prior
warning anywhere in the product. This is a textbook silent data-loss trap and, by virtue of being
customer-facing and consequence-free until an actual disaster, the most dangerous bug found in this audit.

using `db.node`/connection details/decrypted `password` (mirroring `dumpDatabase()`'s approach in

errors instead of swallowing them into a fake success shape, and have restore actually fetch the object
from R2 and pipe it into `psql`/`mysql`/`redis-cli` against the target container.
EOF
echo done

## MEDIUM: DELETE /vps-provisions/:id has no status check -- customers can delete records for still-active VPS, permanently losing panel credentials

File: apps/api/src/routes/vps.ts, `DELETE /vps-provisions/:id` (~line 94-108)
Docstring: *"Remove a terminated VPS provision record (admin/dev or owner)"* -- but the handler never checks
`provision.status`. It's gated only by `canAccessResource(provision.userId, req)`, which (per the
owner-inclusive design confirmed elsewhere in this audit) allows the VPS's own customer-owner to delete it
directly, regardless of whether `status` is `'provisioned'` (active) or `'terminated'`. Since
`credentialRef` (the encrypted panel password) lives only on this row and nowhere else, deleting a
still-`provisioned` record permanently destroys the platform's only record of that VPS's panel URL/
username/password -- the underlying VPS at the upstream provider keeps running (and presumably billing)
with no way for the customer or staff to look up how to reach it again through this platform.
Severity: MEDIUM (real, customer-triggerable, irreversible credential loss for a resource that's still
active; doesn't affect the VPS's provider-side billing/uptime, but does strand the customer's own access).
Suggested fix: require `status === 'terminated'` (matching the docstring) before allowing delete, or route
customer-initiated deletes through an explicit "confirm this VPS has been terminated" step.
EOF
echo done

## CONFIRMED HIGH: git-push deploy webhook never actually checks the pushed branch against the deployment's tracked branch -- any branch push triggers a redeploy from that branch

File: apps/api/src/routes/deployWebhooks.ts, `POST /deploy-webhooks/:deploymentId` (~lines 132-157)
The handler's own comment states the intent explicitly:
> "Only redeploy on a push to the branch this deployment actually tracks (or any branch if none is
> recorded) — a push to an unrelated branch in the same repo shouldn't trigger a rebuild."

But the code that follows never compares `pushedBranch` (parsed from the webhook payload's `ref`) against
`deployment.branch` (a real field on the `Deployment` model, `packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma` line 462).
It unconditionally proceeds to call `buildAndRun(..., { branch: pushedBranch, ... })` for every push to
every branch of the connected repository.

Why it's a bug: pushing to any branch other than the one the deployment is configured to track --
including throwaway feature branches, `dependabot/*` branches, or anyone else's branch in the same repo --
triggers a real rebuild-and-restart of the live deployment using that branch's code, silently overriding
whatever `deployment.branch` says should be running. This is a correctness/safety bug with real production
impact: an unrelated branch push can unexpectedly replace a live production deployment's running code.
Severity: HIGH (silent, easily triggered, directly contradicts the code's own documented intent).
Suggested fix: `if (deployment.branch && pushedBranch && pushedBranch !== deployment.branch) { return res.status(202).json({ accepted: false, reason: 'branch mismatch' }); }` before calling `buildAndRun`.
EOF
echo done

input.command:
cat >> /home/claude/notes/findings.md << 'EOF'

## CONFIRMED HIGH: zip/file-upload deploy endpoint bypasses both subdomain safety checks and node-selection policy that the main deploy path enforces

File: apps/api/src/routes/zipDeployments.ts, `POST /deployments/upload` (~lines 32-98)

**1. Subdomain: no reserved-word check, no uniqueness check, not even the collision-avoidance loop.**
```js
const preferredName = (req.body.preferredName || `upload-app-${Date.now()}`).toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9-]/g, '-');
...
const deployment = await prisma.deployment.create({
  data: { userId: req.user!.id, subdomain: preferredName, repoUrl: `zip://${storageKey}`, branch: 'main', nodeId: node.id },
});
```
Every other deployment-creation path in the codebase runs the chosen name through `generateSubdomain()` /
`validateCustomSubdomain()` (`lib/subdomain.ts`), which rejects reserved names (`www`, `api`, `admin`,
`dashboard`, etc.) and checks for an existing deployment with the same subdomain before use. This endpoint
skips that entirely and writes `preferredName` straight into `Deployment.subdomain`. Since (as found
elsewhere in this audit) `Deployment.subdomain` has no unique DB constraint, two different customers who
both type an ordinary name like `app`, `test`, `demo`, or `api` for their upload -- extremely likely in
practice, not just a low-probability race -- deterministically end up with two live deployments sharing
one hostname, and/or a customer can directly claim a reserved system subdomain (`admin`, `dashboard`,
`api`, ...) that the reserved-word list exists specifically to prevent.

**2. Node selection: customer-supplied `nodeId` is honored directly, with no ownership/tag/active checks.**
```js
const nodeId = req.body.nodeId;
...
const node = nodeId
  ? await prisma.node.findUnique({ where: { id: nodeId } })
  : await prisma.node.findFirst({ where: { isActive: true } });
```
`lib/nodeSelector.ts`'s own docstring states: *"Customer deployments (isAdminDeployment !== true): always
auto-selected. explicitNodeId is ignored even if present — there is no customer-facing way to choose a
node, by design."* -- and `routes/deployments.ts`'s main `POST /deployments` path correctly enforces this
(`effectiveNodeId = effectiveIsAdminDeployment ? data.nodeId : undefined`, then routed through
`selectNodeForDeployment`). `zipDeployments.ts` has no such restriction: any authenticated customer can
supply an arbitrary `nodeId` in their multipart upload and have their deployment placed on that exact
node -- including a node not tagged for general web hosting, or one that isn't even `isActive` (no active
check on the `nodeId`-provided branch either) -- completely bypassing the platform's stated
node-placement policy for this one deployment-creation path.

Severity: HIGH (both issues are directly, deterministically triggerable by an ordinary customer -- no race
condition or special timing required -- and both directly contradict protections the rest of the codebase
enforces for the equivalent Git-based deploy path).
EOF
echo done
